VibePascal v57 Linux x86_64 compiler -- a truncated .ppu is an error, not a hang
Source commit: 1f605f41b3 (merge of otto/ppu-truncated-hang)
Compiler fix:  c31227c8ca  (compiler/entfile.pas)
Parent release: v56 (a187bbac34e1f61154affa5a57e93298028ffc72)
Built: 2026-09-11, native self-host fixpoint on x86_64-linux (stage2 == stage3)
ppcx64 md5:    6A460E0E02CC3EF71313AA5040C1934E
ppcx64 sha256: E22E9AE724C678431F1D4206AE8BEE904CD7504A58B0B447942A8EE9985567D8
ppudump md5:   528F623CD25E9739C690341A85CCC435   (rebuilt: it shares the same reader)

Contents: bin/ppcx64 and bin/ppudump -- a COMPILER-BINARY refresh meant to drop
into an existing VibePascal source/unit tree on Linux.  No RTL change, no
package change, no PPU format change, so an existing v52..v56 Linux unit set
stays valid.  ppudump is included only because it is built from the same reader
that changed; every other utility binary is unchanged and does not need one.

WHAT WAS BROKEN
---------------
Hand the compiler a half-written .ppu and it spun at 99% CPU forever, printed
nothing, and had to be killed.  A zero-byte .ppu was handled correctly and said
so, which is what makes this the compiler's fault rather than the file's.  A
killed build, a full disk or an interrupted copy all leave a partial .ppu
behind; on that input the compiler did not fail your build, it STALLED it, with
no message to grep for.

    intact aspelldyn.ppu   55291 bytes  ->  exit 0 in 0.06s
    zero-byte  .ppu            0 bytes  ->  "Can't find unit", exit 1, instant
    truncated  .ppu          120 bytes  ->  99% CPU, no output, never returns

WHY
---
The PPU reader treated running off the end of the file as a silent no-op: it
returned quietly with the destination buffer untouched and told nobody.  The
entry header is read through that same path, so at end of file the reader still
described the PREVIOUS entry and handed it back to its caller, again and again,
and the interface loader re-processed it forever.  On the 120-byte file the cut
lands exactly at the end of the source-file-list entry, so what got replayed was
the source file list: a million identical "PPU Source:" lines in twelve seconds.

WHAT CHANGED (compiler/entfile.pas, the shared reader, four small changes)
  * reading past end of file sets the reader's error flag -- the exact-fit case,
    where the last byte needed is the last byte present, stays a success;
  * skipping past end of file likewise;
  * on error the entry reader zeroes its entry and reports a read error rather
    than replaying a stale one;
  * end-of-entry reports true once the flag is set, so the seven loops in the
    unit loader that drain an entry stop instead of waiting for data that will
    never arrive.
The compiler already had the right fatal -- "Invalid PPU-File entry" -- and
already stopped on it everywhere; it simply never got told.  No new message, no
message-catalogue change, no PPU format change.  ppudump already guarded itself
with the same error flag, so this makes the compiler agree with its own dump
tool.

MEASURED
--------
Twenty truncation offsets of one real 55291-byte .ppu, identical command line,
only the .ppu varying.  NINE of the twenty hang on v56 -- the reported input was
not special -- and all nine now fail in 0.05s with a message and exit 1:

    offsets 54 70 77 83 100 119 120 121 200 1000   v56 HANG -> v57 exit 1
    offsets 0 1 20 39 40 41 45 27645               unchanged clean error
    intact 55291                                   exit 0 both, still compiles

Full 1983-test corpus A/B against a baseline rebuilt from this same source with
the same command minus the patch: 1983 SAME, 0 DIFF.  Self-host fixpoint
reached, stage2 == stage3 byte-identical.

NOT FIXED, AND NOT HIDDEN
-------------------------
Cutting only the LAST 11 bytes off that 55291-byte file is still accepted with
exit 0: nothing an interface load reads lives in those bytes, so the reader
never notices they are gone.  Catching that needs a whole-file length check
against the size recorded in the header, which must also cope with .ppu data
read from a nonzero offset inside a stream -- a different and riskier change,
deliberately not bundled with a hang fix.

Reported by BuildMaster, who hit it while corrupting a unit on purpose to build
a negative control for something else.
